chapters.title: The Multiplier Effect
chapters.hook: A wrong edition teaches the wrong source. Everyone agreed, but no one knew who would bring back proof.
chapters.counterintuition: The small source line is not clerical. It decides which lesson you are allowed to teach and which proof you still owe.
chapters.tryThisNow: When you cite a source today, circle the edition marker and one fact it permits before you use the claim.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Anchor the source before the lesson: circle the edition marker, separate the 2017 revision from 2010 records, then judge the effect by behavior around people.

breakdown.fastRead:
A wrong edition teaches the wrong source. Everyone agreed, but no one knew who would bring back proof.

In a May 2010 Harvard Business Review article, Liz Wiseman made the Diminisher and Multiplier contrast public with Greg McKeown. That is the early mark. The publisher record for Multipliers gives a later mark: May 16, 2017 is the revised listing.

Mark the source line first. A May 16, 2017 line puts you in the revised edition. If the line says June 15, 2010, you are holding the original record. The wrong record makes a true idea point at the wrong source.
breakdown.deepRead:
Edition comes first because it decides what the claim is allowed to carry. A source can be true and still be the wrong source for the sentence you wrote.

In May 2010, Harvard Business Review carried both named authors under the same article. The article framed two kinds of conduct: Diminishers drain others' intelligence, while Multipliers draw it out. That is not a manners scale. It asks whether people around the person in charge give more judgment, challenge, and follow-through.

Now put that beside the publisher listing. The revised listing carries May 16, 2017 and names 150-plus leaders as its base, plus five disciplines. Those details do different jobs. The HBR article proves the contrast was already public; the 2017 record tells you when the revised source begins. Both can be true. They do not do the same job.

Circle the edition before you teach the claim. The date written where the group reads it can save the idea from the wrong source. Without it, a reader may use the first-release record to defend added revised material, or use the 2017 listing as if it created the whole distinction.

The human part is just as sharp. A Diminisher can be smart and still leave less usable judgment behind. The smartest answer in the room can be the reason the room gets less smart. Who gets smaller after you speak? Watch that evidence, not the self-image.
breakdown.fullRead:
Start with the record that can pay for the sentence. If you teach the revised Multipliers source, the publisher listing with May 16, 2017 has to stand under that sentence. If you teach only the first release, the June 15, 2010 publisher record does a different job.

That sounds like a library chore. It is not. Edition drift is how a careful person makes a false bridge: the idea is real, the source is real, and the join between them is weak. Once the join weakens, the reader cannot tell which added material was actually in view.

The HBR article gives the cleanest guardrail. May 2010 comes before the 2017 revision, and the two named authors are on that public article. So the contrast between Diminisher and Multiplier is not a late invention. A Diminisher drains usable intelligence by making other minds less needed. A Multiplier raises the amount of judgment people bring after contact with that person.

The publisher adds the second guardrail. The revised edition record names the on-sale marker, the data from more than 150 leaders, and five disciplines. Use that record when the claim needs the revised source. Do not ask the 2010 original record to prove what belongs to 2017. A clean number can still point to the wrong shelf.

This is why the productivity claim matters. The promise is not "be nicer and people will feel good." It is doing more with fewer resources by using intelligence already near you. If that sounds soft, look at the evidence you can see after you speak: more thought, more owned effort, more useful challenge. If the answer still comes from one person and others wait, the label did not do much.

You can run the same move without a title. When you cite a file, a training note, or an old record, ask who owes whom what by when. The artifact must tell the same story as the claim. If the source line says 2010, let it prove the 2010 contrast. If the source line says May 16, 2017, let it carry the revised frame. Put the edition mark in place before the lesson starts.

Had they not kept those records apart, three mistakes would follow. The revised edition would look like the birthplace of the Diminisher and Multiplier contrast. The 2010 original record would look strong enough to prove the revised contents. And the research base of more than 150 leaders would shrink in the reader's mind into one good executive tale.

The reversal is simple. You are not checking a source after the lesson; you are checking the source so the lesson has a right to stand. That habit protects the bigger idea. Multiplying is not self-praise. It is the observable change in how others think, decide, and carry effort after dealing with you.

Use the move where the source boundary affects the claim. It does not belong on every low-stakes note, and it can slow a fast handoff. If no added material or version gap is at stake, name the idea and move. If the record will decide what is included, do the opposite: slow down, circle the edition, and keep the marked source line tied to the right source.

examples.title: The Earlier Issue
examples.scenario: A source analyst sees May 2010 as the early signal, but it can hide in plain sight. Liz Wiseman and Greg McKeown already appear under the Harvard Business Review article, on a page that predates the revised listing. The consequence is open: the article proves the contrast is public, but it cannot yet tell which 2017 additions belong to the revised source.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the early mark narrow. Use the HBR article for the public contrast, then require a separate 2017 line for any revised claim.
examples.whyItMatters: Miss this and a true early article starts carrying later material. You protect the contrast by naming what the May 2010 article can and cannot prove.

examples.title: The Revised Standard
examples.scenario: The Multipliers revised listing states the standard: May 16, 2017, more than 150 leaders, five disciplines. That demand costs something. The 2010 record cannot prove revised material, so the easier old identifier loses the job and the 2017 publisher record carries the claim.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the standard and the old identifier will do work it cannot do. Put the May 16, 2017 line beside the revised claim before you cite the broader data.
examples.whyItMatters: Leave the cost unpaid and the revised edition turns into a blur. The hard source line lets the reader know which material is in view.

examples.title: The Original Catch
examples.scenario: A trainer is already pasting the 2010 record into the revised claim. Too late, the Harpercollins catalog finding stops it: the Multipliers original release belongs to June 15, 2010, not to the revised material. Had they not caught that line, the first record would have been made to prove later contents. The miss is barely avoided.
examples.whatToDo: It works because the number has one job. Move the 2010 marker back to the original release, then use the 2017 listing for revised material.
examples.whyItMatters: A late catch still matters. The original record can separate the first source, but it cannot pay for claims added to the later one.

examples.title: The Partial Answer
examples.scenario: At the pass, a source analyst asks what the early article can settle. The May 2010 Harvard Business Review article answers one thing: Liz Wiseman and Greg McKeown had already made the Diminisher and Multiplier contrast public. The move half-works because the article does not settle which revised material came later.
examples.whatToDo: Does the early article settle the revised source? No. Let it prove the contrast, then send added claims back to the May 16, 2017 listing.
examples.whyItMatters: This keeps the win partial. You avoid the false invention claim, but you still need the revised record for what changed after 2010.

examples.title: The Larger Base
examples.scenario: After the source pass, one draft line explains why the single-story version failed: more than 150 leaders. Multipliers ties that scale to the revised listing with May 16, 2017 and five disciplines. The single executive tale loses its lead, and the research base becomes the ground for the claim.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the lone tale before it becomes proof. Let the more than 150 leaders carry the claim, with the May 16, 2017 record beside it.
examples.whyItMatters: One story shrinks the base. The revised listing makes the claim broader, and the cost is that a memorable tale cannot do all the teaching.

examples.title: The Downstream Mix
examples.scenario: A partner downstream first feels the effect when revised material is taught with only the original release attached. The match looks close enough until the Harpercollins catalog finding points back to June 15, 2010 and Multipliers. The miss is caught late, barely, and the claim changes before the reader learns the wrong source boundary.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the wrong boundary before it travels. Pair the original release with original content, then require the revised listing for revised claims.
examples.whyItMatters: Let it travel and the reader pays with confusion. The source boundary is part of the lesson, not a cleanup task after the lesson.

questions.prompt: Your reading group has two Multipliers records open while preparing a handout, and the handout will teach revised material. Which source move comes first?
choices: Use the older identifier if it is easier for the reading group to find.
Start with the May 16, 2017 publisher listing before teaching revised content.
Treat both records as the same since the reading group is teaching one title for this handout.
questions.explanation: The revised listing sets which content belongs to that source. The older-identifier choice is tempting, but it points to the original record and cannot settle revised material.

questions.prompt: When a department is short on staff, a director says Multipliers is mainly about happier employees. What consequence should you predict?
choices: The department may add a comfort program while leaving paid-for capability unused.
The department misses the operating claim: get more output from intelligence already nearby.
The department should ask for headcount first because capability cannot rise inside the current group.
questions.explanation: The model is not only a mood claim. It says unused capability is a resource. The comfort-program answer starts near engagement but stops before output.

questions.prompt: A supervisor stays kind during a budget call but makes every important decision alone before anyone can add judgment. Which principle does that break?
choices: The contrast turns on whether others' judgment is used, not whether the supervisor sounds warm.
The contrast is mostly about whether the supervisor avoids harsh language during tense choices.
The supervisor can count as a Multiplier if the final calls spare others from pressure.
questions.explanation: Kindness is not the test. The key issue is usable intelligence around the person in charge. The warm-language choice mistakes tone for contribution.

questions.prompt: Training notes cite the 2010 original identifier to support a claim about the revised edition. What is the best correction?
choices: Keep the identifier if the training notes also mention that the publisher released the title.
Drop the bibliographic line because source records distract from the leadership idea.
Use the identifier only for the June 15, 2010 original, not as proof of revised contents.
questions.explanation: That identifier marks the original release. It is useful, but not for revised additions. The publisher mention alone does not change which edition it identifies.

questions.prompt: A consultant builds the whole lesson from one memorable executive tale. What should change before the lesson is trusted?
choices: Tie the claim to the revised edition's data from more than 150 leaders.
Keep the executive tale central because one clear story is easier to remember.
Use the publication year alone, since a date proves the research scale.
questions.explanation: The source base is broader than one profile. A single tale may help explain, but it cannot replace the 150-plus-leader base named in the listing.

questions.prompt: During a product call, the smartest person supplies every answer while engineers who know the edge cases stop weighing in. What explains the drop?
choices: The product call needs a sharper expert, since stronger answers raise total intelligence.
One person's brilliance has crowded out judgment that should be coming from others.
The product call should keep decisions with the expert until others feel more ready.
questions.explanation: High intelligence in one person can still lower the total intelligence in use. The sharper-expert answer repeats the error in the product call.

questions.prompt: After a director calls herself empowering during a project reset, the staff still waits for her to make each decision. Which evidence matters most?
choices: Her self-description matters if the staff believes she means it.
Her intent matters more than the staff's behavior after each exchange.
Whether people think harder and own more after interacting with her.
questions.explanation: Self-image is not the measure. The observable effect around her is. The intent answer sounds fair, but it leaves the staff's waiting untouched.

questions.prompt: Someone says they cannot use the Multiplier idea because they are not naturally charismatic. What is the single best reply?
choices: Work on the five disciplines as learnable practices instead of waiting for a new personality.
Use the idea only if charisma is already one of the person's strongest traits in public settings.
Begin with a public confidence boost so the five disciplines feel easier to try.
questions.explanation: The disciplines are framed as learnable. The charisma answer narrows the model to a gift, while the confidence-boost answer changes mood before routine.

questions.prompt: An internal newsletter says the 2017 revision invented the Diminisher and Multiplier distinction. What is the best fix?
choices: Use the original record alone, since it can prove every part of the contrast.
Leave the newsletter as written if it links to the revised publisher listing.
Point to the May 2010 HBR article by Liz Wiseman and Greg McKeown.
questions.explanation: The public article predates the revision and carries both names. The revised listing matters, but it cannot be treated as the origin of the distinction.

reviewCards.front: What should you circle before using a source claim?
reviewCards.back: Circle the edition marker first. The May 16, 2017 publisher listing separates revised material from the 2010 original record.

reviewCards.front: How can the smartest answer reduce the total intelligence in use?
reviewCards.back: When one person centers every answer, others stop adding judgment. The result can be less usable intelligence, even if that one answer is sharp.

reviewCards.front: Why does the more than 150 leaders detail matter?
reviewCards.back: It keeps the framework from shrinking into one executive story. The revised edition presents a broader research base, so a single tale cannot carry the proof.

reviewCards.front: What evidence beats a person's empowering self-image?
reviewCards.back: Look at what happens around that person. If others think harder and own more after the exchange, the effect is visible; the self-label alone is not enough.

reviewCards.front: When does the June 15, 2010 original record help, and when does it fail?
reviewCards.back: It helps identify the first release. It fails when used to prove revised material tied to the 2017 listing.

reviewCards.front: How do learnable disciplines change the reader's action?
reviewCards.back: They move the idea away from natural charisma. You can change routines and practice the five disciplines instead of waiting to become a different kind of person.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Circle the Edition. Before you teach a claim, mark the source line that tells you which version you are using. Then name what that line can prove and what it cannot carry.

ifThenPlans.context: Mark the revised source.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a claim uses revised material, then circle May 16, 2017 before you cite it.

ifThenPlans.context: Fence the original record.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the 2010 original identifier appears, then keep it with the June 15, 2010 original.

ifThenPlans.context: Inspect the effect.
ifThenPlans.plan: If someone claims to multiply others, then look for harder thought and more owned effort around them.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Teach the move to one person in 5 minutes: circle the edition marker on one source line, explain what the mark includes, and ask them to restate it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, count one number: live claims with an edition marker circled before use. Raise the count by one before you add a new source.

chapters.title: The Talent Magnet
chapters.hook: Who pays when the brightest person stays close and the larger challenge goes empty?
chapters.counterintuition: Keeping the best person close can make your orbit less attractive. The pull comes when people know their strongest ability will be named, used, and released when the old role is too small.
chapters.tryThisNow: Schedule 10 minutes: first write one exact strength beside a live assignment, then send the calendar invite for the match talk.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Do not judge talent by who stays near you. Judge it by whether a named strength reaches real stakes and gets released when the role is too small.

breakdown.fastRead:
Satya Nadella took the Microsoft CEO role in 2014 and bet that talent could become a culture test. Someone pays if it stays only a story. The person with unused skill pays first, then the harder challenge pays. Nadella publicly tied Microsoft's renewal to growth mindset, the belief that ability can grow. That question breaks the old sorter: who is smart, who is not, who stays put.

A Talent Magnet, a person whose pull makes ability visible and useful, runs a harsher test. What strength is native here, where should it serve, and when is the old role too small? Praise without placement feels kind. It still wastes the gift. Talent is not proven by who stays near you. It is proven by where capability goes.
breakdown.deepRead:
Talent is fit, not inventory. Native genius means the strength a person keeps bringing before any job title names it. The name matters because it tells you where the strength belongs. Broad praise warms the air for a moment, but a precise label points to the assignment where that skill should be used.

Use this with care. When the stretch is large and the skill is not ready, do the opposite for a while: narrow the task, teach beside it, or keep support close. Calling every stretch good is a softer way to gamble with the person and the result.

Satya Nadella gives the failure a clock. He became Microsoft CEO in 2014, and the same case ties renewal to growth mindset, the belief that ability can be built. Without that handoff, the story floats. With it, the question has a start: will the old rank-and-freeze habit yield to what people can learn and add next?

Google Project Aristotle, an internal study of 180 teams, offers only a side warning here. It highlighted psychological safety, a climate where questions and candor feel less risky. Strong people can withhold doubts, ideas, and mistakes when risk feels too high. The group already has information and still loses it.

The autopsy has three cuts. First, praise stays vague. Next, strong people are attracted but not placed on consequential work. Then the best helper is kept close because release feels like loss. The price is quiet misuse. Hoarding buys ease and spends trust.
breakdown.fullRead:
Nadella's 2014 handoff can be misread as trivia. It is not. The year fixes the moment when Microsoft's culture story has to answer a harder question: did the old fixed-genius frame keep sorting people, or did growth mindset change what capability could become?

Start with the first cut, vague praise. If you call everyone strong, no one knows what should move. Ask a sharper question: which strength keeps showing up, and where would it matter if the assignment were larger? Native genius is not a medal. It is routing information.

The second cut is attraction without use. A place can draw impressive people and still waste them if their best ability sits beside low-stakes tasks. Hiring, access, and warm words are not enough. Who is drawn here because their best skill will meet real stakes, and who is merely stored nearby?

The third cut is captivity. When someone makes the old role easier, keeping that person close feels prudent. That is the counterfeit. A cage is a weak magnet. Real pull grows when capable people trust that growth will not be punished by being trapped.

Pixar's Braintrust, associated with Ed Catmull, shows the same cost in a film setting. Its candid feedback practice gathers peer judgment around unfinished films instead of making one executive command the answer. The film gets more than one title's view. It gets the judgment already gathered near it.

That practice is not a smooth win. Peer critique can leave a story problem more exposed before it is fixed. A growth frame can upset people who liked the old ranks. Release can make the current role harder for a time. Those costs are real, and pretending otherwise makes the move sound cheap.

The failure still teaches the better bargain. A single command may be faster to hear, but it uses less of the ability already present. Hoarding may protect today's comfort, but it teaches strong people that growth leads to capture. Both save ease now and spend trust later.

You can use the small version without title power. When a colleague, friend, or volunteer keeps doing one thing well, do not stop at thanks. Name the strength in plain words. Put it beside a task that matters. If the role is too small, schedule the talk that lets the person grow out of it.

Keep the lesson plain. Talent is not proved by the people you can keep near you. It is proved by the larger challenge that opens once you stop treating people as inventory.

examples.title: The Handoff Check
examples.scenario: Satya Nadella became Microsoft CEO in 2014, and the check is whether the handoff changes the talent frame. Before the move, the culture story can sound like fixed genius: rank people, freeze them, keep the best close. After Nadella publicly ties renewal to growth mindset, the cost lands on that old sorter. Capability has to be judged by what it can learn and add.
examples.whatToDo: Use 2014 as the fixed point: the handoff works by asking what ability can grow and where that ability should go.
examples.whyItMatters: The old rank-and-freeze answer loses control, proving the cost of the change and turning the story into talent use instead of culture talk.

examples.title: The Bare Year
examples.scenario: After the Microsoft story is over, one calendar line keeps the case from going soft: 2014. The miss was close. A retelling could preserve Satya Nadella and growth mindset yet leave capability parked as a slogan. The late fix is to trace the year back to the CEO handoff, then forward to deployment: what strength should the growth frame move into a larger challenge?
examples.whatToDo: Treat 2014 as the hinge between a dated leadership change and the assignment. What does that date keep from going soft? It ties growing capability to the work that should use it.
examples.whyItMatters: A case can be factually dated and still fail if the strength never reaches a consequential assignment. What failure remains after the date is right? Capability can stay preserved instead of deployed.

examples.title: The Film Feels It
examples.scenario: The unfinished Pixar film feels the effect first: the story problem is clearer, not solved. In the Pixar Braintrust associated with Ed Catmull, candid feedback practice lets one peer critique meet another, and no single executive command settles the pass. The turn is spoken through the exchange, but the film still carries the reckoning. Peer judgment has named the problem; the film has not yet answered it.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the peer judgment on the film, not on the rank of the person who raised it.
examples.whyItMatters: The film gets more minds on the problem without making one title the bottleneck.

examples.title: The Unused Circle
examples.scenario: The early signal is easy to miss: strong Pixar peers are near the unfinished film, but their judgment can still stay unused. The Pixar Braintrust associated with Ed Catmull turns presence into deployment. Candid feedback practice puts those minds on the story problem, and the cost is real. Executive command loses speed and comfort because the film now has to face several hard reads.
examples.whatToDo: Stop counting talent as present until its judgment is attached to the problem that needs it.
examples.whyItMatters: Make use visible before status claims credit for ability that never reached the task.

examples.title: The Command Miss
examples.scenario: The standard is stated wrong: make one top creative voice solve the unfinished film. The cut on the screen gets attention, but the Pixar Braintrust move is skipped. Candid feedback practice, the practice associated with Ed Catmull, never reaches the problem. The miss lands there. Strong minds are close enough to help, and the film receives less than they know.
examples.whatToDo: Skipping costs the film candid peer review first; restore it before one senior voice becomes the whole path for judgment.
examples.whyItMatters: A narrower answer is the first waste: useful doubts and ideas stay outside the film.

questions.prompt: When a school club calls every volunteer impressive, then assigns jobs by title, what caused the talent move to fail?
choices: They waited for the faculty sponsor to rank helpers, so the ability label would carry official weight.
They praised the whole club first, so the busiest people could receive the most visible jobs.
They left each strength unnamed, so the club had no guide for where a useful ability should go.
questions.explanation: The failure starts with vague praise. The sponsor-ranking choice sounds orderly, but rank still would not show where a real strength belongs.

questions.prompt: During a neighborhood safety group, skilled members stop asking hard questions. Which priority comes first?
choices: Ask the chair to share the favored view, so later comments can aim at the recognized center of the exchange.
Add one more expert to the group, since the silence may mean the roster lacks skill rather than safety.
Lower the speaking risk, so facts already in the group can surface before choices harden in silence.
questions.explanation: The core problem is hidden information, not a weak roster. Adding another expert misses the fact that useful knowledge is already being withheld.

questions.prompt: A podcast retells Microsoft's renewal with no mention of when Nadella became CEO. What earlier miss weakened the case?
choices: It made growth mindset the full story, so the leadership setting could stay outside the lesson.
It dropped the 2014 CEO handoff, so the culture story lost its fixed point in real time.
It leaned on Nadella's title alone, so rank had to supply the case's weight without a calendar marker.
questions.explanation: The year anchors the CEO transition. Title alone borrows authority, but it does not give the Microsoft culture case its historical start.

questions.prompt: Suppose a community theater's best stage manager has outgrown the role. What should happen first?
choices: Keep the stage manager beside the director until the current show no longer depends on close help from that role.
Open the larger opportunity, since growth should not feel like a penalty for being useful there.
Move the person after any strong week, since release itself proves the theater values talent.
questions.explanation: Release follows outgrown capability. The any-strong-week option fires too soon; it treats release as a signal before the role has become too small.

questions.prompt: After a research circle full of experts misses a flaw, the postmortem shows nobody voiced doubts. What caused the miss?
choices: The experts had information but held it back when candor felt too costly inside the circle.
The circle lacked enough expert status, so more credentials would have changed the discussion.
The senior scientist waited too long to state a view, so the group lacked a center.
questions.explanation: The flaw stayed hidden because risk kept doubts quiet. More credentials would aim at status, while the lost value was information people already had.

questions.prompt: A mutual-aid group recruits impressive volunteers, then gives them filler tasks. Which earlier failure set up the waste?
choices: They looked for release too early, as if any small task proved the group was trapping people.
They let the founding organizer approve every assignment, so rank could protect scarce jobs from newer volunteers.
They treated attraction as success before a real strength met a meaningful assignment.
questions.explanation: The waste began when recruitment counted as the win before deployment. The release choice uses a real move, but from the wrong trigger.

questions.prompt: Before a tutoring program changes how it develops helpers, which order fits the Microsoft lesson?
choices: Sort helpers into lasting tiers, then reserve the hard learners for whoever ranked highest.
Treat ability as buildable first, then ask what each helper can learn and contribute in tutoring.
Borrow Microsoft's language for the handbook, then keep the same fixed labels in daily practice under a new name.
questions.explanation: Growth mindset treats ability as developable. Borrowing the words while keeping fixed labels leaves the old sorting habit in charge.

questions.prompt: A campus group wants one favorite Google story to settle its whole talent rule. Which correction fits the evidence?
choices: Use the 180-team Project Aristotle frame as a broader check, not one vivid story for the campus rule.
Ask the most senior adviser to judge the rule, since local rank can replace a wider sample for the campus group.
Pick the most famous Google group, since a known brand gives enough weight to the lesson.
questions.explanation: Project Aristotle matters here as a broader internal study. A single famous story shrinks the evidence into the exact shortcut the fact warns against.

questions.prompt: In a student film collective, the coordinator wants to solve an unfinished script alone. What maps from Pixar?
choices: Bring candid peers to the script, so several judgments can improve it without one title becoming the bottleneck.
Let the coordinator choose the fix privately, since a single command can spare the script from mixed peer views.
Give every draft broad praise before critique, since warm words can stand in for peer judgment on the script.
questions.explanation: Pixar's Braintrust points to peer critique around unfinished work. The private-fix option repeats the executive-command shortcut this case rejects.

reviewCards.front: What turns praise into useful talent judgment?
reviewCards.back: A precise strength label tells people where the ability belongs. Broad approval may feel warm, but it does not guide assignments or growth.

reviewCards.front: How do you know attraction has become deployment?
reviewCards.back: A capable person is not just nearby or newly recruited. Their strongest contribution is being used on a meaningful challenge.

reviewCards.front: When does release make a talent magnet stronger?
reviewCards.back: Release helps when a person's capability has outgrown the role. Keeping them close may ease today's load, but it teaches people that growth can trap them.

reviewCards.front: What does Microsoft's 2014 CEO handoff add to the lesson?
reviewCards.back: It fixes the culture shift in time and ties the talent lesson to growth mindset. Ability is treated as something people can build, not a rank that freezes them.

reviewCards.front: Why can a group full of experts still miss useful information?
reviewCards.back: If candor feels unsafe, people keep doubts, ideas, and mistakes to themselves. The group loses information its members already had.

reviewCards.front: What does Pixar's Braintrust show about creative judgment?
reviewCards.back: Candid peer review around unfinished films lets several strong minds improve the work without making one executive the sole problem-solver.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Schedule the Strength Match. Before you make a people decision, schedule a short block and write the strength in plain words. Then place it beside a task that matters, or schedule the release talk if the role is already too small.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe broad praise after a strong result; note the ability the praise did not name.
ifThenPlans.plan: If praise stays broad, then schedule 10 minutes to write the exact strength beside one real assignment.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe a capable person doing low-value tasks; note the harder challenge missing that person's strength.
ifThenPlans.plan: If attraction has outrun use, then schedule 10 minutes before adding another small task.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe someone outgrowing a role; note who would gain if the strength moved.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the role is now too small, then schedule the release talk instead of finding another reason to keep the person close.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow ends, schedule 10 minutes and draft the exact line you will use to name one strength and the assignment it should serve.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Friday, if one strength has stayed close but underused, then schedule one assignment or release talk for the coming week.
